title: Coverage of three intervals
html:
Take n=200, p=400, a fixed Gaussian design with correlations 0.5|j−k|, σ=1, and β1=1, β6=0.15, β11=−1, β16=0.15, all other coefficients zero. The targets are a strong coefficient β1, a weak one β6, and β2=0, whose regressor is correlated 0.5 with x1. In each of 1000 data sets we fit the lasso with λ=σ2log⁡p/n=0.245, below 2λ0 for the reason seen in @exm-hd-lasso-bounds, and compute three 95% intervals:

  • the naive interval: least squares on the selected variables and its t interval, reported only when the target was selected;
  • the debiased interval b^j±1.96σ^ωj/n, with node-wise lasso rows (λj=0.024) and σ^2 the lasso residual sum of squares divided by n minus the number of selected variables;
  • the oracle t interval from least squares on the true support plus the target.

The results are in Figure 28.5.1. For the null coefficient β2, the lasso selected x2 in a fraction 0.069 of the data sets, and in those the naive interval covered zero only in a fraction 0.174. For the weak coefficient, selected in a fraction 0.329, the naive coverage was 0.903, and for the strong one 0.915. The debiased intervals covered β1, β6 and β2 in fractions 0.960, 0.946 and 0.940 respectively, close to the oracle’s 0.943, 0.956 and 0.958 for the same three coefficients.

On the strong coefficient the lasso’s average error is −0.210, close to −λ, and the debiased estimate’s is 0.014. The standardized estimates T1 have mean 0.14 and standard deviation 0.95 (panel (a)). Two costs remain.

The debiased intervals are wider than the oracle’s (0.393 against 0.288 for β1): part of this is the price of not knowing the support, and part is tuning. The node-wise penalty λj=0.024, a tenth of 2log⁡p/n, keeps the bound μj≤λj/τ^j2 of @lem-hd-nodewise, and so the remainder, small. But it lets the node-wise fits explain much of each column: τ^j2 (0.28, 0.25 and 0.27 for β1, β6 and β2) is well below the population value 1/(Σ−1)jj, which is 34 for j=1 and 35 otherwise, and that allows a larger ωj (@exr-hd-nodewise-bound).

The second cost is a remainder bias: 0.049 for β2 and 0.046 for the weak β6, about a third of its value. This is the term rj/n of @thm-hd-debiased, at most 𝛃𝛃μj‖β^λ−β‖1, with μj between 0.088 and 0.099 and an average lasso ℓ1 error of 0.74. At n=200 that product is not negligible.
